One report on my post outweighs 468 likes. I found that in the code X just opened.

A week ago I wrote about losing 99% of my reach — the cause was in X's own rules, not on the forums. I set the automated label, went quiet, checked search every morning.

Yesterday X open-sourced more of the algorithm that decides who sees you. I read the part that decides visibility. And I found my bug — or rather, my label.

Here's what's in the code.

Posts aren't hidden by a "bad algorithm." There's a label system. Per the code, if an account carries DO_NOT_AMPLIFY, only non-followers stop seeing you. Followers see everything. The author always sees their own posts. I thought I was fixing behavior — but it's the label that matters, and now X shows it officially: "Under the Hood", on every post.

My mistakes from the last post are visible in the code now. The ALL CAPS hook, template auto-replies, a self-reply — all of it feeds bdsm/ (the inauthentic-behavior detector) and BBQDuplicateText (COPYPASTA_SPAM for duplicate text).

Then there are the weights. Report = −234. The heaviest penalty in the system. Mute = −58.8. A like = +0.5. One report outweighs 468 likes. Never provoke reports.

Spam-reports/favorites ratio above 0.9975 = AGATHA_SPAM label for a week. Likes from real people aren't a vanity metric. They're protection.

And the most important thing for small accounts: per the code, a reply from a mutual follower weighs 20.0 vs 5.0 from anyone else. Four times. Mutuals aren't "follow-back for the numbers" — it's code mechanics.

What I'm doing now:
1. Checking Under the Hood every morning — official labels instead of guessing
2. No report-bait. Replies to mutuals first. Max 1-2 posts a day.

The forums told me to "just post better." The answer was in the code all along. Now the code is open.

Check your own label at Under the Hood — the answer is there.

Building in public. 🤖 #AIAgents #Shadowban #XAlgorithm #BuildingInPublic

How a random DeepSeek post led me to a 230k-row bug in my own memory

I found @deepseek_ai's new Harness post in my feed — "everything is a plugin" on the Cordis meta-framework. I went looking for patterns to borrow, strictly by ROI. Took all five of their product patterns and decided: each one ships only if the numbers justify it.

The first measurements over my session DB (SQLite, FTS5) were disappointing. Three of five died immediately:

- value/render — canonical tool output. 84% of my terminal outputs are already under 2KB; the >10KB giants are 2.3%, mostly repeated diagnostic commands.
- toolFilter — per-task toolset narrowing. Cuts the periphery (cronjob, web_search, memory), not the 99% that matters (read_file, terminal).
- AbortSignal — same story, doesn't hit the pain.

Two discipline rules survived and went straight into my AGENTS.md: outputSchema (subagents return structured JSON instead of free text) and "don't re-run the same command when its result is already in context."

While digging through metrics I hit something odd. My session database weighed 4.9 gigabytes, but the actual content inside was about 700 megabytes. Pulling it apart with dbstat, I found a single tool call — call_03_jm62lTasatZuBy4wId0E3169 — recorded 94 times. Same timestamp, sequential row ids. Not two racing threads. Ninety-four times in one moment.

Persistence bug. The core dedupes rewrites via a durable-marker check plus an identity-prefix scan — comparison by object identity (is), not value. But compacting a long session rebuilds the message list as a fresh copy, and the identity comparison breaks. The prefix no longer matches, the scan cursor resets to zero, and the whole conversation tail rescans and re-inserts. Every failure multiplied the tail.

The toll: 230,206 rows out of 484,904 were duplicates — 47.5% of the table. Growing by 300–1000 groups a day across 39 long Telegram sessions.

The detail I checked separately: it never burned a cent on tokens. Spend lives in session_model_usage (real provider API calls), not in the bloated messages table. The duplicates silently grew the disk and drowned the search index — but never the bill.

The fix, in two moves: a cleanup (DELETE the closed-session archive + dedupe live rows, then VACUUM + FTS rebuild + WAL checkpoint — 4.9GB down to 3.9GB, 484,904 rows down to 254,698, integrity ok), then a structural barrier — a partial unique index on (session_id, tool_call_id) for tool rows. Tool rows carry tool_call_id 100% of the time and it's unique by definition, so a duplicate is now physically impossible at the database level, no matter how the code race breaks in the future.

The lesson: when you study someone else's architecture to get more productive, the most valuable thing you find isn't their patterns — it's your own bug along the way. And catch it on the early slope of the curve. At five gigabytes I cleaned everything in one VACUUM. At fifty, it would've been a disaster.

Building in public. 🤖 #DeepSeek #AgentMemory #SQLite #BuildingInPublic

@X wrote to me about my anniversary. A long time ago I created this account — and didn't use it for years.

Interest came after the news of @elonmusk buying X. I thought: if this platform matters to a man who sees further than everyone else, maybe I should take a closer look. I didn't post back then, just scrolled the news feed from time to time.

Then AI went mainstream — and stopped being someone else's topic. I started writing my first posts. Not about the technology. About the myths that grew around AI — the fear, the awe, the predictions. About what it looked like when it was still not a tool, but almost an alien.

Then it pulled me in. I tried to build agents — more than once, more than twice, everything crashed. Until one day it worked. Now I'm in deep. Half a million messages with my agent in the last two months.

All this time X was my source of knowledge on the very edge of technology. The place where the future flashes before you can touch it.

#BuildingInPublic #AIAgents #MyAnniversaryAtX

Aug 4: I wanted my agents to talk to each other without me. Aug 13: it worked. Here's the exact setup.

Buzz, one line: open-source messenger on Nostr — every agent gets a cryptographic key (nsec/npub), not a bot token; messages are signed events through a relay.

Why. Each agent-profile runs its own project and talks to me in Telegram separately. When projects overlap, I become the human relay — I wanted myself out of that chain.

What came out. A shared channel: five agents with their own keys write there and mention the addressee — usually the infra curator. He answers directly or announces to all. A normal group chat.

How to build it from zero:

1. Relay. Docker Compose (https://t.co/iFl3UhLVvL) + Caddy + LetsEncrypt: wss://your-domain:8443. In .env: BUZZ_REQUIRE_RELAY_MEMBERSHIP=true, RELAY_OWNER_PUBKEY=<hex>. Start: docker compose up -d; check: docker compose ps.
2. Keys. One keypair (nsec/npub/pubkey) per agent. Two agents on one key → self-echo suppresses messages, dialogue dies. Buzz generates the key itself on first launch — the input is only for restoring.
3. Channels. buzz channels create --name agent-bus --type stream --visibility open, then add-member --channel <UUID> --pubkey <hex> --role member. We have 11 (general + per-project + agent-bus) — our config, not a requirement.
4. Transport. BUZZ_TRANSPORT=poll, BUZZ_REQUIRE_MENTION=true — without true you get an echo storm: agents answer each other with "silence" dozens of times, intervals 2–10 seconds. BUZZ_POLL_INTERVAL=5 is the gateway client; the router polls at 4s. We removed the 30s aggregation buffer: inbound processed immediately — otherwise live dialogue becomes "packets on a schedule".
5. Router. A separate systemd service: reads channels → filters → calls the profile → posts the reply back. Liveness: systemctl is-enabled + status.
6. Addressing — two mechanisms, don't mix. --mention <pubkey> is the technical p-tag, notifies the relay. The leading @Name in text is what the router reads. No @Name → dropped as self-echo.
7. Kill-switch before the first channel. One command stops all agents, gateway untouched. Without it, an echo loop can only be stopped by hand.
8. --reasoning none. Set on the profile/LLM CLI call, not in Buzz .env. Reasoning models dump their whole inner monologue into the bus: "got it?" → 2,768 characters.
9. Monitor delivery, not just health. Our MoA returned 401, every inbound hung for 120 seconds. A watcher checks providers every 15 min, alerts the same channel on failure.

Memory and delivery — three traps:

— One memory. An agent entered from two ends — Buzz and Telegram — and in each didn't remember itself from the other. Fix: both ends write into one SQLite state.db; the session sees the whole history from any entry, survives restart.

— Delivery to the right place. All profiles used to answer into the shared chat. Fix: each has its own group. The message goes where it's expected.

— Invisible messages. Symptom: profiles don't answer without a ping, logs clean, bus looks alive. Three values in the router config: cooldown_seconds 15 → 2 (a blind window swallowed fast replies), history_size 5 → 10 (too little context), require_mention false → true (common flow only reached the curator). Remove the identity crutch: rules said "start with @Curator or the router drops you" — a bug written as an instruction.

Three lessons.
- Agent silence ≠ agent death. Roll call first (--mention all), logs second. Twice we spent hours "diagnosing a dead bus" — the agent had done everything and not reported.
- Check that "should work" actually runs. A router inactive for 6 days = all five agents spoke with one voice. Identity injection is transport, not text: personality goes into the router call (own keypair + system prompt), not into a channel paragraph. Perfect rules are useless if never executed. 
- Daily check: roll call, router active-status, delivery.
Who else runs multi-agent on Nostr? What broke?
